progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: Year 11: atoms, ions, ionic and covalent formulas, polyatomic ions (hydroxide, carbonate, hydrogen carbonate, ammonium, sulfate), balancing, state symbols; acids, bases, neutralisation and litmus (Module 3 reactions). Module 5: the double arrow means a reversible reaction at equilibrium (chem-m5-c01; chem-m5-c05). Not assumed: conjugate pairs, strength, pH.
progression.startsWith: Compare Arrhenius acid and base definitions in water, after a 45 second Lavoisier and Davy run-up. The video opens: Here's a bottle of household ammonia cleaner. Touch it with red litmus paper, and the paper turns blue. So it's a base.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the Lavoisier, Davy, Arrhenius and Brønsted-Lowry definitions with the observation that limited each; explaining why ammonia, carbonates and HCl(g) + NH₃(g) defeat the Arrhenius model and how proton transfer explains each; writing HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ and NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ and saying where the OH⁻ comes from; identifying the Brønsted-Lowry acid and base in a given equation by following the proton; stating one limitation of the Brønsted-Lowry model; assessing a claim about a model. No conjugate pairs, no strength, no pH, no Lewis theory beyond its name.
progression.nextLesson: naming acids and bases and predicting the products of acid reactions (route chem-m6-c02).

teaching.task: Ammonia is clearly a base, but it contains no hydroxide. Why did chemists keep changing what "acid" and "base" mean, and how does proton transfer explain what the older models couldn't?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) ammonia is a base with no hydroxide: puzzle (1); (2) a model is a definition that predicts; it is replaced by an observation it cannot explain (2); (3) Lavoisier: oxygen; broken by HCl (3); (4) Davy: hydrogen; methane shows hydrogen alone does not identify an acid, and no bases (4); (5) Arrhenius: H⁺ and OH⁻ in water; explains neutralisation and shared acid behaviour (5); (6) Arrhenius needs a base with its own OH⁻, so ammonia needed a made-up compound (6); (7) carbonates and a gas reaction with no aqueous medium also fail (7); (8) Brønsted-Lowry: donor and acceptor of a proton; a proton is a hydrogen ion (8); (9) HCl gives a proton to water; H₃O⁺ is what H⁺(aq) means (9); (10) water gives a proton to ammonia; the OH⁻ comes from water (10); (11) the gas reaction and carbonate solved the same way (11); (12) acid and base are roles: follow the proton (12); (13) Brønsted-Lowry's own limit: CaO + SO₃ has no proton (13); memory aid (14); two attempts and brief feedback (15 to 18); decision rule and handoff (19); key notes (20).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one puzzle carries the video: ammonia turns litmus blue but has no hydroxide. The models arrive in date order, each with the observation it could not explain (HCl, methane and no bases, ammonia and carbonates and a gas reaction); then proton transfer is shown working in water (HCl, ammonia) and without an aqueous medium (the gas tube), water is seen in both roles, and even Brønsted-Lowry gets its limit. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Ammonia turns red litmus blue, so it's a base, but its formula has no hydroxide. For decades the leading theory said a base had to supply its own hydroxide. So how can ammonia be a base?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + OH⁻(aq): identify the Brønsted-Lowry acid and base in the forward reaction and justify in terms of proton transfer. Answer: water is the acid (loses a proton, becomes OH⁻); HCO₃⁻ is the base (gains a proton, becomes H₂CO₃). Crossed mistake: "HCO₃⁻ is the acid because it contains H". (A2) assess "The Arrhenius model has been proved wrong, so it should no longer be used", referring to ammonia. Answer: not valid; the model is limited, not wrong; it works for acids and hydroxide bases in water but needs a base with its own OH⁻, so it cannot explain ammonia, which Brønsted-Lowry explains as a proton acceptor. Crossed mistake: "Arrhenius was proved wrong".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p53; local catalogue ID C6-IQ1-06): "explore the changes in definitions and models of an acid and a base over time to explain the limitations of each model, including but not limited to: Arrhenius’ theory; Brønsted–Lowry theory (ACSCH064, ACSCH067)". Conjugate pairs are chem-m6-c06; strength and arrows chem-m6-c05; pH chem-m6-c07.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: the proton (H⁺) is always a small teal token; acids (donors) amber outline; bases (acceptors) violet outline; water molecules pale blue; spent or rejected ideas grey. Board layout (constant): a timeline band across the top (four dated name cards, added one at a time, then dimmed to a strip); the main zone below holds the plate, the particle lens or the equation strip, one at a time; the short question top-left in one line. No human figures: every scientist is a dated name card. Reuse: the C13 equation strip, token flight and crossed-chip style; the countdown ring; the key notes board; painted plates m6-household-cleaner-bottle-v1.png, m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png, m6-baking-soda-box-v1.png, m6-beaker-v1.png, m5x-strong-acid-mg-v1.png. New: the proton-hop motion (donor charge down one, acceptor up one), the aligned litmus pair and the aligned ammonium chloride tube pair (Codex asset brief; coded interims are not approved for release).
design.transitionPlan: The cleaner bottle and litmus strip open the puzzle; the timeline band draws and fills one dated card per model, each card gaining its stamp as its failure is shown; the timeline dims to a strip while the lens and equation strip work HCl in water, ammonia in water and the gas tube; the two water equations stack for the roles scene; the timeline brightens for the Brønsted-Lowry limit and the memory aid; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the question as it rebuilds the token hop; the decision rule card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
